danish.title: Niende bog (1812) — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Selv om Balasjov var vant til kejserlig pragt, blev han forbløffet over luksussen og pragten ved Napoleons hof.

Grev de Turenne førte ham ind i en stor modtagelsessal, hvor mange generaler, kammerherrer og polske magnater — hvoraf adskillige havde Balasjov set ved den russiske kejsers hof — ventede. Duroc sagde, at Napoleon ville modtage den russiske general, før han red ud.
Efter nogle minutter kom den kammerherretjeneste, der var på vagt, ind i den store modtagelsessal og bad, idet han bøjede sig høfligt, Balasjov om at følge med.

Balasjov gik ind i et lille forværelse, hvor en dør førte ind til et arbejdsværelse — det selv samme, hvorfra den russiske kejser havde sendt ham af sted på sit ærinde. Han stod et minut eller to og ventede. Han hørte hastende skridt bag døren, begge dørfløje blev hurtigt slået op; alt var stille, og så hørtes lyden af andre skridt fra arbejdsværelset, faste og beslutsomme — det var Napoleons. Han var netop blevet klædt på til sin ridetur og bar en blå uniform, der var åben fortil over en hvid vest, så lang at den dækkede hans runde mave, hvide læderbukser der sad stramt på de fede lår af hans korte ben, og ridestøvler. Hans korte hår var tydeligvis netop børstet, men en lok hang ned midt på den brede pande. Hans fyldige, hvide hals stak skarpt frem over uniformens sorte krave, og han duftede af eau de cologne. Hans fyldige ansigt, temmelig ungdommeligt, med den fremtrædende hage, bar et nådigt og majestætisk udtryk af kejserlig velkomst.

Han trådte raskt ind med et ryk ved hvert skridt og hovedet let kastet tilbage. Hele hans korte, fyldige skikkelse med brede, tykke skuldre og bryst og mave, der uvilkårligt buede fremad, havde det imponerende og statelige udseende, man ser hos mænd på fyrre, der lever i bekvemmelighed. Det var også tydeligt, at han var i det bedste humør den dag.

Han nikkede som svar på Balasjovs dybe og ærbødige buk og gik straks hen til ham og begyndte at tale som en mand, der værdsætter hvert øjeblik af sin tid og ikke nedlader sig til at forberede, hvad han vil sige, men er sikker på altid at sige det rigtige og sige det godt.
»Goddag, general!« sagde han. »Jeg har modtaget det brev, De bragte fra kejser Aleksandr, og er meget glad for at se Dem.« Han rettede sine store øjne mod Balasjovs ansigt og så straks forbi ham.

Det var tydeligt, at Balasjovs person slet ikke interesserede ham. Åbenbart var det kun det, der foregik i hans eget sind, der interesserede ham. Intet uden for ham selv havde nogen betydning for ham, fordi alt i verden, syntes han, udelukkende afhang af hans vilje.
»Jeg ønsker ikke krig, og har ikke ønsket den,« fortsatte han, »men den er blevet påtvunget mig. Selv nu« (han understregede ordet) »er jeg rede til at modtage enhver forklaring, De kan give mig.«

Og han begyndte klart og kortfattet at forklare sine grunde til utilfredshed med den russiske regering. At dømme efter den roligt afdæmpede og venlige tone, hvori den franske kejser talte, var Balasjov fast overbevist om, at han ønskede fred og agtede at indlede forhandlinger.

Da Napoleon, efter at have talt færdig, spørgende så på den russiske udsending, begyndte Balasjov en tale, han længe havde forberedt: »Sire! Kejseren, min herre...« men synet af kejserens øjne rettet mod ham bragte ham ud af fatning. »De er nervøs — tag Dem sammen!« syntes Napoleon at sige, idet han med et knap mærkbart smil betragtede Balasjovs uniform og sabel.

Balasjov samlede sig og begyndte at tale. Han sagde, at kejser Aleksandr ikke betragtede Kurákins krav om sine pas som tilstrækkelig grund til krig; at Kurákin havde handlet på eget initiativ og uden sin herskers samtykke, at kejser Aleksandr ikke ønskede krig og ikke stod i forbindelse med England.
»Endnu ikke!« indskød Napoleon, og som om han frygtede at give sine følelser frit løb, rynkede han panden og nikkede let som tegn på, at Balasjov kunne fortsætte.

Da Balasjov havde sagt alt, han var blevet instrueret om at sige, tilføjede han, at kejser Aleksandr ønskede fred, men ikke ville indlede forhandlinger undtagen på den betingelse, at... Her tøvede Balasjov: han huskede de ord, kejser Aleksandr ikke havde skrevet i sit brev, men som han særskilt havde indsat i reskriptet til Saltykóv og havde bedt Balasjov gentage for Napoleon. Balasjov huskede disse ord — »Så længe en eneste bevæbnet fjende befinder sig på russisk jord« — men en indviklet følelse holdt ham tilbage. Han kunne ikke sige dem, selv om han ønskede det. Han blev forvirret og sagde: »På betingelse af at den franske hær trækker sig tilbage bag Njemen.«

Napoleon lagde mærke til Balasjovs forlegenhed, da han sagde disse sidste ord; hans ansigt fortrak sig, og lægmusklen på hans venstre ben begyndte at dirre rytmisk. Uden at flytte sig fra, hvor han stod, begyndte han at tale i en højere tone og hurtigere end før. Under den tale, der fulgte, sænkede Balasjov, der mere end én gang slog øjnene ned, uvilkårligt blikket mod den dirrende bevægelse i Napoleons venstre ben, som blev stærkere, jo mere Napoleon hævede stemmen.

»Jeg ønsker fred, ikke mindre end kejser Aleksandr,« begyndte han. »Har jeg ikke i atten måneder gjort alt for at opnå den? Jeg har ventet atten måneder på forklaringer. Men hvad kræves der af mig for at indlede forhandlinger?« sagde han med rynket pande og en energisk spørgende gestus med sin lille, hvide, fyldige hånd.
»Tilbagetrækning af Deres hær bag Njemen, sire,« svarede Balasjov.
»Njemen?« gentog Napoleon. »Så nu vil I have mig til at trække mig tilbage bag Njemen — kun Njemen?« gentog Napoleon og så lige på Balasjov.
Denne bøjede ærbødigt hovedet.
I stedet for kravet fire måneder tidligere om tilbagetrækning fra Pommern krævedes nu kun en tilbagetrækning bag Njemen. Napoleon vendte sig hurtigt om og begyndte at gå frem og tilbage i værelset.

»De siger, at kravet nu er, at jeg skal trække mig tilbage bag Njemen, før forhandlingerne kan begynde, men for bare to måneder siden var kravet, at jeg skulle trække mig tilbage bag Wisła og Oder, og alligevel er De villig til at forhandle.«

Han gik tavst fra det ene hjørne af værelset til det andet og standsede igen foran Balasjov. Balasjov lagde mærke til, at hans venstre ben dirrede hurtigere end før, og at hans ansigt syntes forstenet i sit strenge udtryk. Denne dirren i hans venstre ben var noget, Napoleon selv var bevidst om. »Min venstre lægs sitren er et stort tegn hos mig,« bemærkede han ved en senere lejlighed.

»Sådanne krav om at trække sig bag Wisła og Oder kan man stille til en fyrste af Baden, men ikke til mig!« næsten skreg Napoleon, til sin egen overraskelse. »Hvis I gav mig Petersborg og Moskva, kunne jeg ikke acceptere sådanne betingelser. De siger, jeg har begyndt denne krig! Men hvem samlede først sin hær? Kejser Aleksandr, ikke jeg! Og De tilbyder mig forhandlinger, når jeg har brugt millioner, når I er i alliance med England, og når jeres stilling er dårlig. De tilbyder mig forhandlinger! Men hvad er formålet med jeres alliance med England? Hvad har hun givet jer?« fortsatte han hastigt, tydeligvis ikke længere for at vise fordelene ved fred og drøfte dens mulighed, men kun for at bevise sin egen retfærdighed og magt og Aleksandrs fejl og bedrag.

Indledningen af hans tale var åbenbart gjort med den hensigt at vise fordelene ved hans stilling og påvise, at han ikke desto mindre var villig til at forhandle. Men han var begyndt at tale, og jo mere han talte, jo mindre kunne han styre sine ord.
Hele meningen med hans bemærkninger var nu tydeligvis at ophøje sig selv og fornærme Aleksandr — netop det, han mindst havde ønsket ved samtalens begyndelse.
»Jeg hører, I har sluttet fred med tyrkerne?«
Balasjov bøjede bekræftende hovedet.
»Freden er sluttet...« begyndte han.
Men Napoleon lod ham ikke tale. Han ville åbenbart selv føre hele samtalen og fortsatte med den veltalenhed og uhæmmede irritabilitet, som forkælede mennesker er så tilbøjelige til.

»Ja, jeg ved, I har sluttet fred med tyrkerne uden at få Moldavien og Valakiet; jeg ville have givet jeres hersker disse provinser, ligesom jeg gav ham Finland. Ja,« fortsatte han, »jeg lovede og ville have givet kejser Aleksandr Moldavien og Valakiet, og nu vil han ikke have disse pragtfulde provinser. Dog kunne han have forenet dem med sit rige og i løbet af en enkelt regeringstid udvidet Rusland fra Den Botniske Bugt til Donaus munding. Katarina den Store kunne ikke have gjort mere,« sagde Napoleon, der blev mere og mere ophidset, mens han gik frem og tilbage i værelset og næsten gentog de selvsamme ord, han havde brugt over for Aleksandr i Tilsit. »Alt det ville han have skyldt mit venskab. Åh, hvilken pragtfuld regeringstid!« gentog han flere gange, hvorefter han holdt inde, tog en guldsnustobaksdåse op af lommen, løftede den til næsen og snusede grådigt.
»Hvilken pragtfuld regeringstid kejser Aleksandr kunne have haft!«
Han så medfølende på Balasjov, og så snart denne forsøgte at komme med en indsigelse, afbrød han ham hastigt.

»Hvad kunne han ønske eller søge, som han ikke ville have opnået gennem mit venskab?« spurgte Napoleon og trak på skuldrene i forvirring. »Men nej, han har foretrukket at omgive sig med mine fjender, og med hvem? Med Stein, Armfeldt, Bennigsen og Wintzingerode! Stein, en forræder fordrevet fra sit eget land; Armfeldt, en udsvævende og intrigant; Wintzingerode, en flygtet fransk undersåt; Bennigsen, lidt mere soldat end de andre, men alligevel en uduelig, der ikke formåede noget i 1807 og som burde vække forfærdelige minder hos kejser Aleksandr... Lad os antage, at de var dygtige, så kunne man bruge dem,« fortsatte Napoleon, der knap kunne holde trit i ord med den strøm af tanker, der uophørligt væltede frem og beviste, hvor ret han havde og hvor stærk han var (i hans opfattelse var de to ét og det samme), »men det er de ikke engang! De duer hverken til krig eller fred! Barclay siges at være den dygtigste af dem alle, men det kan jeg ikke sige, at dømme efter hans første bevægelser. Og hvad laver de alle disse hoffolk? Pfuel foreslår, Armfeldt bestrider, Bennigsen overvejer, og Barclay, der er kaldet til at handle, ved ikke, hvad han skal beslutte, og tiden går uden resultat. Bagratión alene er militærmand. Han er dum, men han har erfaring, et hurtigt øje og beslutsomhed... Og hvilken rolle spiller jeres unge hersker i denne uhyrlige skare? De kompromitterer ham og lægger ansvaret for alt, hvad der sker, på hans skuldre. En regent bør ikke være med hæren, medmindre han er general!« sagde Napoleon og udtalte tydeligvis disse ord som en direkte udfordring til kejseren. Han vidste, hvor meget Aleksandr ønskede at være feltherre.
»Felttoget begyndte for kun en uge siden, og I har ikke engang kunnet forsvare Vilna. I er skåret over i to og er blevet drevet ud af de polske provinser. Jeres hær knurrer.«
»Tværtimod, Deres Majestæt,« sagde Balasjov, der næppe kunne huske, hvad der var blevet sagt til ham, og med besvær fulgte dette ordgyteri, »tropperne brænder af iver...«

»Jeg ved alt!« afbrød Napoleon ham. »Jeg ved alt. Jeg kender antallet af jeres bataljoner lige så nøjagtigt, som jeg kender mine egne. I har ikke to hundrede tusind mand, og jeg har tre gange så mange. Jeg giver Dem mit æresord,« sagde Napoleon og glemte, at hans æresord ikke kunne have nogen vægt — »jeg giver Dem mit æresord på, at jeg har fem hundrede og tredive tusind mand på denne side af Wisła. Tyrkerne vil ikke gavne jer; de duer ikke til noget og har vist det ved at slutte fred med jer. Hvad angår svenskerne — det er deres skæbne at blive styret af vanvittige konger. Deres konge var sindssyg, og de byttede ham ud med en anden — Bernadotte, som straks blev vanvittig — for ingen svensker ville alliere sig med Rusland, medmindre han var sindssyg.«
Napoleon grinede ondskabsfuldt og løftede igen snustobaksdåsen til næsen.

Balasjov vidste, hvordan han skulle svare på hver af Napoleons bemærkninger, og ville have gjort det; han gjorde hele tiden den gestus, en mand gør, når han ønsker at sige noget, men Napoleon afbrød ham altid. Til den påståede vanvittighed hos svenskerne ville Balasjov have svaret, at når Rusland er på dens side, er Sverige praktisk talt en ø: men Napoleon kom med et vredt udbrud for at overdøve ham. Napoleon var i den ophidselsestilstand, hvor et menneske er nødt til at tale og tale og tale blot for at overbevise sig selv om, at han har ret. Balasjov begyndte at føle sig utilpas: som udsending frygtede han at nedværdige sin værdighed og følte nødvendigheden af at svare; men som menneske veg han tilbage for det transporterede raseri af grundløs vrede, der tydeligvis havde grebet Napoleon. Han vidste, at ingen af de ord, Napoleon nu ytrede, havde nogen betydning, og at Napoleon selv ville skamme sig over dem, når han kom til besindelse. Balasjov stod med sænket blik og fulgte bevægelserne af Napoleons buttede ben, mens han forsøgte at undgå at møde hans øjne.
»Men hvad rager jeres allierede mig?« sagde Napoleon. »Jeg har allierede — polakkerne. Der er firs tusind af dem, og de kæmper som løver. Og der vil blive to hundrede tusind.«

Og sandsynligvis endnu mere foruroliget over, at han havde udtalt denne åbenbare usandhed, og at Balasjov stadig stod tavs foran ham i den samme holdning af underkastelse under skæbnen, vendte Napoleon sig brat om, trådte tæt hen til Balasjovs ansigt og gestikulerede hurtigt og energisk med sine hvide hænder og næsten råbte:

»Vid, at hvis I ophidser Preussen imod mig, visker jeg det ud fra Europas kort!« erklærede han med blegt ansigt, forvrænget af vrede, og slog energisk den ene lille hånd mod den anden. »Ja, jeg vil kaste jer tilbage bag Dvina og Dnjepr og genrejse mod jer den barriere, det var forbryderisk og blindt af Europa at tillade at blive ødelagt. Ja, det er, hvad der vil ske med jer. Det er, hvad I har opnået ved at fremmedgøre mig!« Og han gik tavst flere gange frem og tilbage i værelset, mens hans fede skuldre rystede.

Han stak snustobaksdåsen i vestelommen, tog den op igen, løftede den flere gange til næsen og standsede foran Balasjov. Han holdt inde, så ironisk lige ind i Balasjovs øjne og sagde med stille stemme:
»Og dog, hvilken pragtfuld regeringstid jeres herre kunne have haft!«

Balasjov følte det som sin pligt at svare og sagde, at fra russisk side så tingene ikke så mørke ud. Napoleon tav og så stadig hånligt på ham og lyttede tydeligvis ikke. Balasjov sagde, at man i Rusland ventede de bedste resultater af krigen. Napoleon nikkede nedladende, som om han ville sige: »Jeg ved, det er din pligt at sige det, men du tror det ikke selv. Jeg har overbevist dig.«

Da Balasjov var færdig, tog Napoleon igen sin snustobaksdåse op, snuste til den og stampede to gange i gulvet som signal. Døren åbnedes, en kammerherre overrakte ærbødigt kejseren hans hat og handsker; en anden bragte ham et lommetørklæde. Napoleon vendte sig mod Balasjov uden at skænke dem et blik:

»Forsikr kejser Aleksandr fra mig,« sagde han, idet han tog sin hat, »at jeg er lige så hengiven mod ham som før: jeg kender ham til bunds og sætter den største pris på hans høje egenskaber. Jeg vil ikke opholde Dem længere, general; De vil modtage mit brev til kejseren.«
Og Napoleon gik hurtigt mod døren. Alle i modtagelsesværelset styrtede fremad og ned ad trappen.

english.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Balashev was used to imperial splendor, but the luxury and magnificence of Napoleon's court still amazed him.

The Comte de Turenne led him into a large reception room, where many generals, gentlemen-in-waiting and Polish magnates were waiting — several of them men Balashev had seen at the Russian Emperor's court. Duroc told him that Napoleon would receive the Russian general before going out for his ride.
A few minutes later the gentleman-in-waiting on duty came into the great reception room, bowed politely, and asked Balashev to follow him.

Balashev went into a small reception room. One of its doors opened into a study — the very one from which the Russian Emperor had sent him on his mission. He stood there a minute or two, waiting. Beyond the door he heard hurried footsteps, and both halves of it were swung quickly open. Then everything went quiet, and from the study came the sound of other steps, firm and resolute. They were Napoleon's. He had just finished dressing for his ride. He wore a blue uniform open at the front over a white waistcoat, which was so long that it covered his rounded stomach, along with white leather breeches that fitted tightly over the fat thighs of his short legs, and Hessian boots. His short hair had plainly just been brushed, yet one lock hung down the middle of his broad forehead. His plump white neck stood out sharply above the black collar of his uniform, and he smelled of Eau de Cologne. His full, rather youthful face, with its prominent chin, wore a gracious and majestic look of imperial welcome.

He came in briskly, jerking with every step, his head slightly thrown back. His whole short, corpulent figure — broad thick shoulders, chest and stomach thrusting forward of their own accord — had the imposing, stately air you see in men of forty who live in comfort. It was also clear that he was in the best of spirits that day.

He nodded in answer to Balashev's low, respectful bow and came straight up to him. He began speaking at once, like a man who prizes every moment of his time, who does not bother to prepare what he will say, and who is sure he will always say the right thing and say it well.

"Good day, General!" he said. "I have received the letter you brought from the Emperor Alexander, and I am very glad to see you." His large eyes glanced into Balashev's face and immediately looked past him.

It was plain that Balashev as a person did not interest him at all. Evidently only what went on in his own mind interested him. Nothing outside himself had any significance for him, because everything in the world, it seemed to him, depended entirely on his will.
"I do not want war, and I never did," he went on, "but it has been forced on me. Even now" (he stressed the word) "I am ready to hear any explanations you can give me."

And he began to set out, clearly and concisely, his reasons for being dissatisfied with the Russian government. The French Emperor spoke in a calm, moderate and friendly tone, and judging by it, Balashev became firmly convinced that he wanted peace and meant to enter into negotiations.

When Napoleon finished and looked questioningly at the Russian envoy, Balashev began a speech he had prepared long before: "Sire! The Emperor, my master..." But the sight of the Emperor's eyes fixed on him threw him into confusion. "You are flustered — compose yourself!" Napoleon seemed to say, as he glanced at Balashev's uniform and sword with a barely noticeable smile.

Balashev recovered and began to speak. He said that the Emperor Alexander did not regard Kurakin's demand for his passports as sufficient cause for war; that Kurakin had acted on his own initiative, without his sovereign's consent; that the Emperor Alexander did not want war and had no ties with England.
"Not yet!" Napoleon cut in. As if afraid of giving vent to his feelings, he frowned and gave a slight nod, a sign that Balashev might go on.

Having said everything he had been instructed to say, Balashev added that the Emperor Alexander wanted peace but would not enter into negotiations except on condition that... Here Balashev hesitated. He remembered the words that the Emperor Alexander had left out of his letter but had specially inserted in the rescript to Saltykov, telling Balashev to repeat them to Napoleon. Balashev remembered these words — "So long as a single armed foe remains on Russian soil" — but some complicated feeling held him back. He wanted to say them and could not. He grew confused and said instead: "On condition that the French army withdraws beyond the Niemen."

Napoleon noticed Balashev's embarrassment as he spoke these last words. His face twitched, and the calf of his left leg began to quiver rhythmically. Without moving from where he stood, he began to speak more loudly and more hurriedly than before. During the speech that followed, Balashev lowered his eyes more than once, and he could not help noticing the quivering of Napoleon's left leg, which grew stronger the more Napoleon raised his voice.

"I want peace no less than the Emperor Alexander does," he began. "Haven't I spent eighteen months doing everything I could to get it? I have waited eighteen months for explanations. But what is demanded of me before negotiations can begin?" he said, frowning and making an energetic questioning gesture with his small, white, plump hand.
"The withdrawal of your army beyond the Niemen, sire," replied Balashev.
"The Niemen?" repeated Napoleon. "So now you want me to retreat beyond the Niemen — only the Niemen?" He repeated it again, looking straight at Balashev.
Balashev bowed his head respectfully.
Four months earlier the demand had been to withdraw from Pomerania; now only a withdrawal beyond the Niemen was asked. Napoleon turned sharply and began to pace the room.

"You say the demand now is that I withdraw beyond the Niemen before negotiations begin. But in exactly the same way, two months ago, the demand was that I withdraw beyond the Vistula and the Oder — and yet you are willing to negotiate."

He walked in silence from one corner of the room to the other, then stopped in front of Balashev again. Balashev saw that his left leg was quivering faster than before and that his face seemed frozen in its stern expression. Napoleon was aware of this quivering of his left leg. "The vibration of my left calf is a great sign with me," he remarked at a later date.

"Demands to retreat beyond the Vistula and the Oder may be made to a Prince of Baden, but not to me!" Napoleon almost screamed, to his own surprise. "If you gave me Petersburg and Moscow, I could not accept such conditions. You say I started this war! But who joined his army first? The Emperor Alexander, not I! And you offer me negotiations when I have spent millions, when you are in alliance with England, and when your position is a bad one. You offer me negotiations! But what is the point of your alliance with England? What has she given you?" He went on hurriedly. He was evidently no longer trying to show the advantages of peace or discuss whether it was possible. He only wanted to prove his own rightness and power, and Alexander's errors and duplicity.

He had plainly begun his speech meaning to show how strong his position was and that he was nonetheless willing to negotiate. But once he started talking, the more he talked, the less he could control his words.
The whole drift of his remarks was now evidently to exalt himself and insult Alexander — exactly what he had least wanted at the start of the interview.
"I hear you have made peace with Turkey?"
Balashev bowed his head in agreement.
"Peace has been concluded..." he began.
But Napoleon would not let him speak. He evidently wanted to do all the talking himself, and he went on with the kind of eloquence and unrestrained irritability that spoiled people are so prone to.

"Yes, I know you have made peace with the Turks without getting Moldavia and Wallachia. I would have given your sovereign those provinces, as I gave him Finland. Yes," he went on, "I promised the Emperor Alexander Moldavia and Wallachia and would have given them to him, and now he won't have those splendid provinces. Yet he could have joined them to his empire and, in a single reign, stretched Russia from the Gulf of Bothnia to the mouths of the Danube. Catherine the Great could not have done more," said Napoleon. He grew more and more excited as he paced up and down the room, repeating to Balashev almost the very words he had used to Alexander himself at Tilsit. "He would have owed all that to my friendship. Oh, what a splendid reign!" he repeated several times. Then he stopped, took a gold snuffbox from his pocket, raised it to his nose, and sniffed at it greedily.
"What a splendid reign the Emperor Alexander's might have been!"
He looked at Balashev with compassion, and as soon as Balashev tried to make some reply, he hastily cut him off.

"What could he wish or look for that he would not have got through my friendship?" demanded Napoleon, shrugging his shoulders in perplexity. "But no, he has preferred to surround himself with my enemies — and with whom? With Steins, Armfeldts, Bennigsens, Wintzingerodes! Stein, a traitor driven out of his own country; Armfeldt, a rake and an intriguer; Wintzingerode, a fugitive French subject; Bennigsen, rather more of a soldier than the others, but all the same an incompetent who could do nothing in 1807, and who ought to awaken terrible memories in the Emperor Alexander's mind.... Granted, if they were competent they might be made use of," Napoleon continued. He could hardly keep pace in words with the rush of thoughts that kept springing up, all proving how right and strong he was (in his mind the two were one and the same). "But they aren't even that! They are fit neither for war nor for peace! Barclay is said to be the ablest of them all, but judging by his first movements I cannot say so. And what are they doing, all these courtiers? Pfuel proposes, Armfeldt argues, Bennigsen considers, and Barclay, called on to act, does not know what to decide, and time passes and brings no result. Bagration alone is a military man. He's stupid, but he has experience, a quick eye and resolution.... And what part is your young monarch playing in that monstrous crowd? They compromise him and make him answerable for everything that happens. A sovereign should not be with the army unless he is a general!" Napoleon said, evidently flinging these words as a direct challenge to the Emperor. He knew how much Alexander wanted to be a military commander.
"The campaign began only a week ago, and you haven't even been able to defend Vilna. You are cut in two and have been driven out of the Polish provinces. Your army is grumbling."

"On the contrary, Your Majesty," said Balashev. He could hardly remember what had been said to him and followed this display of verbal fireworks with difficulty. "The troops are burning with eagerness..."

"I know everything!" Napoleon interrupted. "I know everything. I know the number of your battalions as exactly as I know my own. You do not have two hundred thousand men, and I have three times that many. I give you my word of honor," said Napoleon, forgetting that his word of honor could carry no weight — "I give you my word of honor that I have five hundred and thirty thousand men this side of the Vistula. The Turks will be of no use to you; they are worth nothing, and they have shown it by making peace with you. As for the Swedes, it is their fate to be governed by mad kings. Their king was insane, so they changed him for another — Bernadotte, who promptly went mad — for no Swede would ally himself with Russia unless he were mad."
Napoleon grinned maliciously and again raised his snuffbox to his nose.

Balashev knew how to answer each of Napoleon's remarks and would have done so. Again and again he made the gesture of a man who wants to speak, but Napoleon always cut him off. To the alleged insanity of the Swedes, Balashev wanted to reply that when Russia is on her side, Sweden is practically an island. But Napoleon gave an angry exclamation to drown his voice. Napoleon was in that state of irritability in which a man has to talk, and talk, and talk, merely to convince himself that he is in the right. Balashev began to feel uncomfortable. As an envoy, he feared to demean his dignity and felt he must reply; as a man, he shrank before the fit of groundless rage that had evidently seized Napoleon. He knew that none of the words Napoleon was now uttering meant anything, and that Napoleon himself would be ashamed of them when he came to his senses. Balashev stood with downcast eyes, watching the movements of Napoleon's stout legs and trying to avoid meeting his eyes.
"But what do I care about your allies?" said Napoleon. "I have allies — the Poles. There are eighty thousand of them and they fight like lions. And there will be two hundred thousand of them."

He was probably even more thrown by the fact that he had just told such an obvious falsehood, and that Balashev still stood silent before him in the same attitude of submission to fate. Napoleon abruptly turned round, came close to Balashev's face, and, gesturing rapidly and energetically with his white hands, almost shouted:

"Know that if you stir up Prussia against me, I'll wipe it off the map of Europe!" he declared, his face pale and distorted with anger, and he struck one of his small hands energetically with the other. "Yes, I will throw you back beyond the Dvina and beyond the Dnieper, and I will rebuild against you that barrier which Europe was criminal and blind to let be destroyed. Yes, that is what will happen to you. That is what you have gained by alienating me!" And he walked silently up and down the room several times, his fat shoulders twitching.

He put his snuffbox into his waistcoat pocket, took it out again, raised it to his nose several times, and stopped in front of Balashev. He paused, looked ironically straight into Balashev's eyes, and said in a quiet voice:
"And yet what a splendid reign your master might have had!"

Balashev felt he had to reply, and said that from the Russian side things did not look so gloomy. Napoleon was silent, still looking at him with derision and evidently not listening. Balashev said that in Russia the best results were expected from the war. Napoleon nodded condescendingly, as if to say, "I know it's your duty to say that, but you don't believe it yourself. I have convinced you."

When Balashev had finished, Napoleon took out his snuffbox again, sniffed at it, and stamped his foot twice on the floor as a signal. The door opened. A gentleman-in-waiting bowed respectfully and handed the Emperor his hat and gloves; another brought him a pocket handkerchief. Napoleon turned to Balashev without giving them a glance:

"Assure the Emperor Alexander from me," he said, taking his hat, "that I am as devoted to him as before. I know him thoroughly, and I think very highly of his lofty qualities. I will not detain you any longer, General; you shall receive my letter to the Emperor."
And Napoleon went quickly to the door. Everyone in the reception room rushed forward and down the staircase.
